title: Respiratory substrates and RQ; respirometers; Plant transport: phloem and translocation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RS05#t2 term and clue written for the game; EX11#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX11#t2 term and clue written for the game; RS05#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX11#N.5, RS05#N.7, EX11#N.8, RS05#N.9, EX11#N.12a, RS05#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Potassium hydroxide
items.clue: Alkali solution placed in the tube to absorb CO₂.

items.label: Companion cell
items.clue: Has a nucleus, dense cytoplasm and many mitochondria; makes the ATP needed for loading.

items.label: Sieve plate
items.clue: Perforated end wall between phloem tube elements, full of pores so sap can flow through.

items.label: Control
items.clue: Tube of glass beads of the same volume, correcting for temperature and pressure changes.

questions.stem: Which feature of a sieve tube element helps sap to flow along the phloem?

options.text: It is dead and empty like a xylem vessel, so there is nothing inside the cell to slow the flow of sap.
Its end walls are solid plates that hold the sap under pressure so that it flows faster along the tube.
It contains many mitochondria, whose ATP is used to push the sap along the tube towards the sink.
It has lost its nucleus and most of its cytoplasm and organelles, so little inside it obstructs the sap.

questions.stem: In a respirometer, carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide. With 5.0 g of germinating seeds, the gas volume in the apparatus fell by 1.2 cm³ in 10 minutes. What is the rate of respiration per gram?

options.text: 0.024 cm³ of carbon dioxide produced per gram per minute
0.12 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen given out per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute

questions.explanation: The fall in volume equals the oxygen consumed, as the alkali removes carbon dioxide. 1.2 ÷ 10 ÷ 5.0 = 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.

questions.stem: In spring, sugars stored in the roots of a deciduous tree are converted to sucrose and carried in the phloem to the opening buds. Which statement about this transport is correct?

options.text: Mitochondria in the companion cells provide the ATP that physically drives the sap along the sieve tubes up to the buds.
Companion cells in the root use ATP to load sucrose into the sieve tubes, and the sap flows up to the buds, the sinks.
Sap cannot move upwards in the phloem, so the sugars must instead be carried up to the buds in the xylem.
The sieve tube elements must first be killed and emptied, as in xylem, before any sap is able to flow through them.

questions.stem: Yeast in a respirometer was studied for 10 minutes. With potassium hydroxide present, the bead moved towards the yeast by a volume of 45 mm³. Without potassium hydroxide, the bead moved away from the yeast by 9 mm³. What is the RQ?
questions.explanation: O₂ used = 45. Moving away means CO₂ released = 45 + 9 = 54. RQ = 54 ÷ 45 = 1.2. Above 1: some anaerobic respiration.

questions.stem: A young leaf near a shoot tip is still expanding. It imports sucrose through the phloem. Weeks later, fully grown, the same leaf exports sucrose. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Now it makes more sugar than it uses, so its companion cells load sucrose: it has become a source.
When young, the leaf received its sugar in the xylem, because phloem only ever carries sap out of leaves.
As the leaf aged, its sieve tubes died and became lignified, which reversed the direction of flow.
Mitochondria in the leaf's companion cells switched from pushing sap in to pushing sap out.

questions.stem: Illustrative data. A student measured oxygen uptake by yeast (cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹) at five temperatures: 20 °C 0.10; 30 °C 0.19; 40 °C 0.31; 50 °C 0.26; 60 °C 0.04. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Rate rises with temperature over the whole range, so the low reading at 60 °C must be an experimental error.
Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum near 40 °C, then falls as the enzymes of respiration denature.
Above 40 °C the yeast switches to anaerobic respiration, which uses no oxygen, so oxygen uptake falls.
At 60 °C the extra carbon dioxide produced expands and pushes the liquid back, hiding the true rate.
